title: Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1st generation)
verdict: Chevrolet showed up late to the Bronco-and-Scout party, so it brought a bigger truck: a half-ton pickup with the back cut off and the roof made optional. Four model years, one full-length lift-off top and a parts bin shared with every Chevy pickup made it the one rivals had to answer.

paragraphs: By 1969 Ford had the [[bronco/early-bronco|Bronco]], International had the [[scout/scout-80-800|Scout]] and Jeep had the [[jeep/cj-5|CJ-5]], and General Motors had nothing in the small, go-anywhere class. Chevrolet's answer was not small at all. The K5 Blazer took the half-ton K10 4x4 pickup, cut the wheelbase from 115 to 104 inches, and gave it a removable top. Wikipedia credits that pickup basis with three advantages over the rivals: more cargo room, a better on-road ride from the wider track and longer wheelbase, and lower cost, because most of the parts were already on a production line.

story.heading: A PICKUP WITH THE BACK CUT OFF
paragraphs: MotorTrend's history of the K5 puts it bluntly: Ford had the Bronco, Jeep had the CJ, even a tractor company had the Scout, and GM had nothing. Basing the Blazer on the short-box K10 let Chevrolet reach the market quickly and with more capability than the competition. The base truck was spartan to the point of comedy. MotorTrend notes that early base Blazers came without a roof or a passenger seat, so the driver had the only seat in the house.

Underneath it was all 1969 Chevy truck: a ladder frame, tapered leaf springs at both ends, a Dana 44 front axle and a GM 12-bolt rear. Chevrolet's 1969 spec sheet lists 8 inches of ground clearance, a 35-degree approach angle, a 25-degree departure angle, a 23.5-gallon tank and a 5,000 lb maximum GVW. Engines matched the pickups: the 250 six as standard, a 307 V8, and the 350 V8, which came only with the four-speed SM465 or the Turbo Hydra-Matic 350.

story.heading: THE TOP COMES OFF
paragraphs: The first-generation Blazer is the only K5 whose whole roof comes off. MotorTrend describes a completely removable hardtop that left only the windshield sticking up. Chevrolet's 1971 brochure describes the auxiliary top as reinforced fiberglass with textured paint in black or white, with side rear windows and a lift tailgate, and says it 'bolts on' and 'lifts off quickly.' A canvas soft top on steel framing was a dealer-installed accessory. Chevrolet claimed it went up or down in under two minutes.

The 1973–75 Blazers on the new [[chevrolet/k5-blazer|square-body chassis]] kept a fully removable top. From 1976 a fixed steel roof covered the front seats and only the rear section came off. If you want to drive with nothing above you but sky and the windshield header, the 1969–72 trucks are where the K5 story begins. They're also the shortest K5s, at 177.5 to 180 inches against 184.8 for the 1973 truck, which helps on tight trails.

story.heading: THE 1971–72 TRUCKS
paragraphs: The changes came fast. For 1970 Chevrolet added a two-wheel-drive Blazer with coil-spring independent front suspension, and GMC got its own version, the Jimmy. For 1971, power front disc brakes became standard across GM's light trucks, replacing four-wheel drums. The 1971 truck also got an egg-crate grille and grew to 180 inches long. That year's brochure pushed the CST package: bucket seats, a console, chrome bumpers, extra insulation and deep-twist carpet.

For 1972 the 292 six disappeared from the option list, and the 350 was rated at 175 net horsepower. Then sales took off. CK5's model-year figures show production going from 4,935 in 1969 to 44,266 in 1972, matching MotorTrend's claim that sales grew roughly tenfold over the first generation. In April 1970 Car and Driver wrote, and Chevrolet happily quoted in its 1971 brochure, that someone had finally discarded the idea that four-wheel-drive vehicles could only be operated by ex-tank commanders and veteran truck drivers.

story.heading: WHY IT MATTERS
paragraphs: Wikipedia says the Blazer had overtaken its rivals by 1970. Dodge answered with the Ramcharger and Jeep with the SJ Cherokee for 1974, and in 1978 Ford moved the [[bronco/full-size|Bronco]] onto a shortened F-100 platform specifically to fight the K5. The truck-based SUV recipe that the [[chevrolet/k5-blazer|later K5]], the Tahoe and nearly every full-size SUV since have followed starts with these four model years.

Today the early Blazer and Jimmy are serious collector trucks. Recent Bring a Trailer results for original-spec examples run from the mid-$20,000s to $100,000, with resto-mods higher still. Parts are easy because so much is shared with 1967–72 Chevy and GMC pickups, and reproduction sheet metal and seals are plentiful. Rust and tired frames are where the money goes, so buy the best body you can afford and fix the drivetrain later.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE GMC VERSION
callout.title: GMC Jimmy: same truck, different badge
paragraphs: GMC got the truck for the 1970 model year and called it the Jimmy, a long-standing nickname for GMC itself. MotorTrend says the two were essentially identical apart from a few styling tweaks.

GMC's 1971 brochure lists four series: CE-1550 and CS-1550 for two-wheel drive, and KE-1550 and KS-1550 for 4x4. The 4x4s were rated at 4,600–5,000 lb GVW and used the same engines as the Chevrolet: the 250 six and the 307 and 350 V8s. Tires ran from E78-15B as standard up to 10-16.5 on the 4x4s. On Bring a Trailer the Jimmy is the cheaper way into a first-gen truck. Original Jimmys have sold for about $24,000–72,000 since 2025.

engineering_intro: The first K5 is a 1969–72 K10 half-ton 4x4 shortened to a 104-inch wheelbase. It has a ladder frame, tapered leaf springs at all four corners, a Dana 44 front axle and a GM 12-bolt semi-floating rear. The engine drives through a three- or four-speed manual or a TH350 automatic to a two-speed transfer case, which is either a Dana 20 or a New Process 205. The open body takes a full-length fiberglass hardtop or a canvas soft top.

engineering.v: Shortened K10 ladder frame, 104 in wheelbase
engineering.note: Cut down from the 115 in half-ton pickup. 177.5 in long in 1969, 180 in from 1971.
Open-knuckle Dana 44 with manual locking hubs (BaT 1969 listing). 3.73 gears standard, 3.07 optional with the 350.
8.875 in ring gear per CK5's spec sheet. Positraction was optional.
The Dana 20 (2.03:1 low) came only with manuals. The gear-driven NP205 (1.96:1 low) came with the automatic and was optional with manuals.
1971 ratings: 110, 135 and 170 net hp. The 292 six is listed for 1970–71. The 350 was rated at 175 net hp for 1972.
Textured fiberglass hardtop in black or white, or a dealer canvas top. The only K5 generation with no fixed roof.

generations_table.note: Launch year. Four-wheel drums, top and passenger seat optional. 4,935 built.
Two-wheel-drive Blazer and the GMC Jimmy arrive. New grille with six groups of 'dashes'. 11,527 built.
Power front disc brakes standard. Egg-crate grille, 180 in length. 17,220 built.
292 dropped. Grille surround no longer black. 44,266 built.
GMC grille and badging. 4,600–5,000 lb GVW on the 4x4s (1971 brochure).

buying_checks.head: Rust first, drivetrain second
buying_checks.body: Velocity Restorations lists the floorboards, wheel wells, inner fenders and door bottoms as the usual rust spots. The Drive adds the top of the windshield frame. Fresh paint can hide all of it, so bring a magnet and look underneath.

buying_checks.head: Inspect the frame at the steering box
buying_checks.body: Offroad Design says straight-axle GM trucks are notorious for frame cracks where the steering box mounts, especially with lifts, big tires and off-road use. Look for cracks and old weld repairs on the driver's-side rail ahead of the front axle.

buying_checks.head: Is the top there, and does it fit?
buying_checks.body: Many first-gen trucks have lost their hardtop or soft top. The Drive notes that the fiberglass top's textured finish is hard to match in repairs. Check the top's mounting edge, the liftgate and the seals, because a leaky or missing top is expensive to sort out.

buying_checks.head: Work out what has been swapped
buying_checks.body: Recent BaT results include LS, Vortec, 383, 454 and 6.2 L swaps alongside original trucks. Velocity advises caution unless swap work is documented and done by a qualified builder. Decide whether you're paying for originality or for the build.

buying_checks.head: Read the SPID decal
buying_checks.body: Factory equipment and paint are listed on the Service Parts Identification decal inside the glovebox, per a 1969 BaT listing. Use it to check a claimed CST, Positraction or V8 truck.

buying_checks.head: Expect a loose chassis
buying_checks.body: The Drive warns that the chassis is flexible and the steering has play, and that a big power upgrade can make the handling worse. Budget for steering-box, tie-rod and bushing work, and drive it before you agree a price.

buying_checks.head: Check which transfer case and hubs it has
buying_checks.body: Manual trucks may have the Dana 20 or the NP205. Automatic trucks have the NP205. Offroad Design notes the NP205's tag sits above the front output and that the case is one piece of cast iron. Make sure the hubs lock and unlock.

buying_checks.head: Mind the brakes on 1969–70 trucks
buying_checks.body: Front discs became standard for 1971. Earlier trucks have four-wheel drums unless they've been converted, so ask what has been changed and how well it was done.

repairs.title: Brace the steering box mount before the frame cracks
repairs.cost: Parts plus a drill and basic hand tools
repairs.symptoms: Steering that wanders or clunks, the steering box moving on the frame when someone saws at the wheel, or visible cracks around the box mounting bolts on a lifted or big-tire truck.
repairs.fix: Clean and inspect the frame rail around the box mounting area first, since a crack needs welding before a brace. Offroad Design's bolt-in brace for 1967–72 GM 4WD trucks triangulates the box mount to the crossmember and frame. It bolts on, but you have to drill one hole. Follow ORD's instructions, which note that some frames need washers to space the brace out. Re-torque everything after the first few drives.
repairs.tools: Drill and bits · socket set · torque wrench · wire brush · ORD instructions PDF

parts.name: Bolt-in steering box brace for '67–72 GM 4WD trucks
Bolt-in brace clip and hardware only, '67–72 GM

repairs.title: Reseal the hardtop, liftgate and doors
repairs.symptoms: Water on the floors after rain or a car wash, wind noise at speed, or rust starting under old seals.
repairs.fix: Remove the old rubber and scrape the channels back to clean metal and fiberglass. Treat any surface rust you find. Fit new hardtop quarter-glass seals, door-opening weatherstrip and the liftgate seal with weatherstrip adhesive, working a short section at a time. Refit the top and check the fit at the bedsides before you tighten the bolts fully. Water-test with a hose.
repairs.tools: Plastic scrapers · adhesive remover · weatherstrip adhesive · masking tape · garden hose

parts.name: Hardtop quarter-glass seal, LH or RH, 69–72 Blazer/Jimmy

repairs.title: Cut out and replace rotten floors, rockers and wheelhouses
repairs.cost: Panels are cheap; welding time isn't
repairs.symptoms: Soft or perforated floor pans, bubbling rockers and door bottoms, or rotten rear inner wheelhouses. These are the areas Velocity Restorations and The Drive flag.
repairs.fix: Strip the interior and get the truck on stands with the doors shut, so the body doesn't move. Cut out one area at a time and leave sound metal to weld to. Trial-fit the reproduction panel, then plug- or butt-weld it in short stitches to avoid warping. Seam-seal and prime, and cavity-wax the rockers once they're closed up. For anything structural, measure the door gaps before and after.
repairs.tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · seam sealer · weld-through primer

repairs.title: Repack front wheel bearings and replace spindle seals
repairs.symptoms: Play at the top and bottom of the tire, a growl that changes as you turn, or grease and water inside the hub after deep water.
repairs.fix: Lift and support the front, then remove the wheel, the brake and the locking hub. Remove the spindle nuts and slide the hub off. Clean everything, inspect the races, and replace the bearings, races and hub seal as a set if anything is pitted. Pack the new bearings with grease, refit, set the preload per the shop manual and fit a new spindle seal while you're in there.
repairs.tools: Spindle-nut socket · bearing race driver · grease packer · torque wrench · shop manual

parts.name: GM Dana 44 and Corporate 10-bolt wheel bearing kit, Timken (per side)
GM Dana 44 and Corporate 10-bolt spindle seal and bearing kit, all years (per side)

repairs.title: Replace worn locking hubs
repairs.symptoms: Hubs that won't engage, pop out in four-wheel drive, or let the front driveshaft spin in two-wheel drive.
repairs.fix: With the truck on stands, remove the hub cover bolts and pull the old hub body and inner drive gear. Clean the hub and spindle area, check the bearings while it's apart, and install the new hub with the gasket and hardware supplied. Test both positions by hand, then on a slippery surface. Offroad Design sells Yukon Hardcore hubs for 1978-and-older GM Dana 44s (19-spline). Confirm the spline count on yours first.
repairs.tools: Hex or socket bits · snap-ring pliers · grease · torque wrench

parts.name: Yukon Hardcore locking hub set, '78 and older Dana 44, GM & Ford, 19-spline

repairs.title: Rebush the leaf springs and shackles
repairs.symptoms: Clunks over bumps, vague steering, a truck that leans or sits low on one side, or cracked rubber at the spring eyes and shackles.
repairs.fix: Support the frame and take the weight off one spring at a time. Remove the shackle and eye bolts, burn or press out the old bushings and fit the new ones. Offroad Design's leaf-spring bushing page lists which bushing fits each spring position. If the truck leans, ORD's advice is to measure the free arch of the springs on the floor and swap them side to side before blaming the spring rate. Torque the bolts with the truck at ride height.
repairs.tools: Floor jack and stands · press or bushing tool · torch for old rubber · penetrating oil · torque wrench

parts.name: Universal 1969–1991 full vehicle bushing kit with HD front shackles
Front and rear leaf spring bushings

repairs.title: Service the brakes (drums to 1970, front discs from 1971)
repairs.symptoms: A pull to one side, a low or spongy pedal, or seeping wheel cylinders. Also any truck that has sat for years.
repairs.fix: Inspect every hose and steel line, since old trucks rust their lines from the outside. On 1969–70 trucks rebuild or replace the wheel cylinders, fit new shoes and adjust the drums. On 1971–72 trucks fit new pads and inspect the calipers and rotors. Bleed with fresh fluid from the wheel farthest from the master cylinder inward. Stainless front hoses are worth fitting on a lifted truck.
repairs.tools: Line wrenches · drum adjuster tool · bleeder kit · fresh brake fluid

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: On a 67-72 Chevy Trucks thread about a stock 1972 Blazer, several owners run 33x12.50s on 15x8 wheels. Others call 32x11.50 the limit if the springs have sagged. One owner found 33x14.50s rubbed the springs, so width matters as much as height. On CK5, a member calls 33s about 2 inches bigger than stock 31s, fine for a while on the road but likely to hit off-road.

faq.q: What's the difference between a K5 Blazer and a GMC Jimmy?
faq.a: Badging and trim. GMC started selling the Jimmy for 1970, and MotorTrend calls the two essentially identical apart from a few styling tweaks. GMC's 1971 brochure lists 4x4 Jimmys as KE-1550 and KS-1550, with the same 250, 307 and 350 engines as the Chevrolet.

faq.q: Does the whole roof really come off?
faq.a: Yes. On 1969–72 trucks the hardtop is a full-length fiberglass shell that bolts on and lifts off, leaving just the windshield. A canvas soft top was a dealer accessory. From 1976 the K5 had a fixed roof over the front seats and only the rear section came off.

faq.q: Which engines did it come with?
faq.a: The 250 six was standard, with the 307 and 350 V8s optional. A 292 six is listed for 1970–71. Chevrolet's 1971 brochure rates the 250, 307 and 350 at 110, 135 and 170 net horsepower (145, 200 and 250 gross). CK5 lists 175 hp for the 1972 350.

faq.q: Which transfer case do I have?
faq.a: The Dana 20 came only with manual transmissions. The NP205 was fitted with the automatic and offered with manuals too. Offroad Design says the 205 is one piece of cast iron, with a small three-bolt idler cover on the back and an ID tag above the front output.

faq.q: When did it get disc brakes?
faq.a: For 1971, when power front disc brakes became standard across GM's light trucks. 1969–70 trucks have drums at all four corners unless they've been converted.

Yes. Wikipedia says the 2WD version was added for 1970, and CK5 says fewer than 1,000 were built that year. It used coil-spring independent front suspension and coil springs with trailing arms at the rear, so check for a front driveshaft before you assume a truck is a 4x4.
CK5's spec sheet gives 4,935 for 1969, 11,527 for 1970, 17,220 for 1971 and 44,266 for 1972. Wikipedia lists the same numbers but flags them as uncited.

faq.q: What axle gears did it have, and should I regear for bigger tires?
faq.a: The 1971 spec sheet lists 3.73 gears as standard on the 4x4, with 3.07 optional on V8 trucks. Owners on CK5 warn that 33s feel big with 3.08s. Offroad Design generally recommends gearing a lifted truck deeper to keep the engine in its useful rev range.
Six lugs on 5.5 inches, shared with 1967–87 half-ton GM 4x4s. That makes period wheels and later GM 6-lug wheels easy to find, but check backspacing before buying.

On Bring a Trailer, original-spec first-gen Blazers and Jimmys sold for about $24,000–100,000 between March 2025 and October 2026, with a median a little under $50,000. Resto-mods with modern engines have reached $146,000–170,000.

mods.why: Fresh springs fix sagging 50-year-old leaves and clear 33s or 35s. Offroad Design builds custom-arc springs specifically for 1969–72 GM trucks.

mods.why: Brace the box mount first. Bigger tires then call for crossover steering, which moves the draglink up and out of the way.

The 12-bolt is a good axle. Gears, lockers and axle shafts are all still made.
Floors, rockers, wheelhouses and every rubber seal on the top are reproduced.

baseline_service.intro: Assume a 50-year-old truck's fluids are any age and its rubber is original until proven otherwise. Baseline everything, then deal with the frame, steering and brakes before you trust it on a trail. Factory capacities for 1969–72 weren't available from sources we could verify, so check the Chevrolet shop manual for those.

items.interval: Now, then every 3,000–5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: Check which engine you actually have: many trucks now run a later small-block or an LS.

items.item: Ignition: points or HEI, cap, rotor, plugs, wires
items.spec: Points gap and timing [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: Points ignition was original. Many owners convert to a GM HEI distributor, as on BaT's 1972 Highlander truck.

items.spec: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: The 1969–72 option lists included heavy-duty cooling with air conditioning or an automatic. Upgraded aluminum radiators are common on restored trucks.
1969–70 trucks have four-wheel drums and 1971–72 trucks power front discs. Replace any rusty steel line rather than patching it.

items.spec: SM465 / 3-speed manual or TH350 automatic [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: On a TH350, drop the pan and change the filter, then check for metal in the pan.

items.spec: NP205: 80W-90 gear oil per CK5 members, filled to just below the fill hole · Dana 20 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: Identify the case first. The 205 is a one-piece iron case with a three-bolt idler cover on the back (Offroad Design).
